nameStory: Tussock cottongrass gets its charming name from its fluffy white seed heads that look exactly like cotton balls dancing in the breeze. The "tussock" part refers to how this plant grows in dense, bumpy clumps that create little hillocks in wetlands. It's also called hare's-tail cottongrass because the white, fluffy seed heads resemble a rabbit's cottony tail.
description: Tussock cottongrass is a striking wetland plant that creates distinctive clumps or "tussocks" in boggy areas. Growing 1-2 feet tall, it produces grass-like leaves and gorgeous white, cotton-ball seed heads that wave gracefully in the wind. Despite its common name, it's actually a sedge, not a grass, and belongs to the same family as bulrushes. The plant is most noticeable and beautiful when those fluffy white plumes appear, transforming wet meadows into what looks like a field of natural cotton balls.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: Single white, fluffy cotton-ball plumes top each stem - unmistakable when present. The cottony fluff feels soft and silky to the touch, and individual strands will blow away if you gently disturb them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, bumpy tussocks or clumps that create small mounds in wetlands. These clumps feel firm underfoot and can be 8-12 inches across, rising above the surrounding wet ground.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves emerge from the base in tight clusters. The leaves feel somewhat stiff and have a distinctive triangular cross-section if you roll them between your fingers.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, upright stems rise 1-2 feet tall with each stem topped by a single seed head. The stems feel firm and slightly triangular when you run your fingers along them.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous brownish flowers appear before the showy white seed heads develop. The flowers cluster tightly together in a small spike at the stem tip.

habitat: Look for tussock cottongrass in acidic bogs, fens, and other wet, spongy areas throughout New England's mountains and cooler regions. It thrives in nutrient-poor, acidic soils and is often found alongside sphagnum moss, bog laurel, and other bog plants. You'll typically find it in higher elevation wetlands, alpine zones, and northern bogs where the soil stays consistently moist and acidic.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from the tussocks, and small brownish flower spikes begin to form at stem tips. The plant starts its growth spurt as wetland areas thaw.
seasonality.summer: The magical transformation happens as flowers give way to the spectacular white, fluffy seed heads that make this plant famous. Peak "cotton ball" display occurs in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads begin to disperse as individual cotton strands blow away in the wind. Leaves start to turn golden-brown and become less prominent.
seasonality.winter: The distinctive tussock mounds remain visible above snow and ice, appearing as raised bumps in the frozen wetland landscape. Old stem bases may persist.

funFact: Each "cotton ball" contains hundreds of seeds, and a single plant can produce over 20,000 seeds per year - meaning one small tussock could theoretically populate an entire wetland! The cottony fluff isn't just for show; each strand acts like a tiny parachute that can carry seeds for miles on the wind.
confusionNotes: The white fluffy seed heads are so distinctive that tussock cottongrass is hard to confuse with anything else when in seed. Before the cotton appears, it might be confused with other sedges or grasses, but the distinctive tussock growth habit is a dead giveaway - remember "bumpy clumps in bogs."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "cottongrass," this plant is actually a sedge, not a true grass. The "cotton" isn't cotton either - it's specialized bristles called perigynia that help seeds disperse. This naming confusion is common with many plants that look grass-like but belong to the sedge family.
compareHints: Tussock cottongrass is the only cottongrass that grows in distinctive single tussocks and produces just one seed head per stem. Common cottongrass has multiple fluffy heads per stem and doesn't form the characteristic bumpy mounds. The other New England cottongrasses also lack the prominent tussock-forming habit that makes this species so distinctive in wetland landscapes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cottongrasses, tawny cottongrass is unique for its brown seed heads - common cottongrass and tussock cottongrass both have white or cream-colored fluff.
Among New England's cottongrasses, green-keeled stands out with its bright white seed heads and prominently ridged leaves.
Rough cottongrass is the smallest and most delicate of New England's cottongrasses.
Common cottongrass typically has multiple nodding seed heads per stem, while tussock cottongrass usually has just one erect cottony head per stem.
Among New England's cottongrasses, slender cottongrass stands out for its thin, delicate build and preference for the wettest bog conditions.
